claim: Androgen receptor (AR) is a master regulator essential for prostate development and tumorigenesis.
source: In the prostate, androgen receptor (AR) is a master regulator essential for development and tumorigenesis, but its specific functions in prostate stem/progenitor cells have not been elucidated.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge about AR's role in prostate biology.

claim: CARNs (CAstration-Resistant Nkx3.1-expressing cells) are a luminal stem/progenitor cell that functions in prostate regeneration.
source: We have investigated AR function in CARNs (CAstration-Resistant Nkx3.1-expressing cells), a luminal stem/progenitor cell that functions in prostate regeneration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information about CARNs, supported by prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Progenitor properties of CARNs are largely unaffected by AR deletion, apart from decreased proliferation in vivo.
source: Using genetically--engineered mouse models and novel prostate epithelial cell lines, we find that progenitor properties of CARNs are largely unaffected by AR deletion, apart from decreased proliferation in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experiments with genetically-engineered mice and cell lines.

claim: AR loss suppresses tumor formation after deletion of the Pten tumor suppressor in CARNs.
source: Furthermore, AR loss suppresses tumor formation after deletion of the Pten tumor suppressor in CARNs
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experiments with genetically-engineered mice.

claim: Combined Pten deletion and activation of oncogenic Kras in AR-deleted CARNs result in tumors with focal neuroendocrine differentiation.
source: however, combined Pten deletion and activation of oncogenic Kras in AR-deleted CARNs result in tumors with focal neuroendocrine differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experiments with genetically-engineered mice.

claim: AR modulates specific progenitor properties of CARNs, including their ability to serve as a cell of origin for prostate cancer.
source: Our findings show that AR modulates specific progenitor properties of CARNs, including their ability to serve as a cell of origin for prostate cancer.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Both luminal and basal cells are mostly lineage-restricted (unipotent) in the normal adult mouse prostate.
source: Lineage-tracing studies have shown that both luminal and basal cells are mostly lineage-restricted (unipotent) in the normal adult mouse prostate as well as during androgen-mediated prostate regeneration (Choi et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cells within the basal compartment possess stem/progenitor properties in a range of ex vivo assays as well as during inflammation and wound repair.
source: In addition, cells within the basal compartment possess stem/progenitor properties in a range of ex vivo assays as well as during inflammation and wound repair (Goldstein et al., 2008; Höfner et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2014; Lawson et al., 2007; Toivanen et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by multiple citations.

claim: Luminal cells can display stem/progenitor properties in specific in vivo and ex vivo contexts.
source: However, recent studies have shown that luminal cells can also display stem/progenitor properties in specific in vivo and ex vivo contexts (Chua et al., 2014; Karthaus et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is considerable evidence supporting a luminal origin for prostate cancer in mouse models.
source: Furthermore, there is now considerable evidence supporting a luminal origin for prostate cancer, both in mouse models (Wang et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2014) as well as in human tissues (Gurel et al., 2008; Meeker et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by citations.

claim: There is considerable evidence supporting a luminal origin for prostate cancer in human tissues.
source: Furthermore, there is now considerable evidence supporting a luminal origin for prostate cancer, both in mouse models (Wang et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2014) as well as in human tissues (Gurel et al., 2008; Meeker et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by citations.

claim: AR is primarily expressed by luminal cells in the prostate epithelium of adult hormonally intact mice.
source: In the prostate epithelium of adult hormonally intact mice, AR is primarily expressed by luminal cells, but is also found in a subset of basal cells (Lee et al., 2012; Mirosevich et al., 1999; Xie et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by citations.

claim: AR is found in a subset of basal cells in the prostate epithelium of adult hormonally intact mice.
source: In the prostate epithelium of adult hormonally intact mice, AR is primarily expressed by luminal cells, but is also found in a subset of basal cells (Lee et al., 2012; Mirosevich et al., 1999; Xie et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by citations.

claim: Conditional deletion of AR in the adult prostate epithelium results in a short-term increase in proliferation of luminal cells.
source: Several studies have shown that conditional deletion of AR in the adult prostate epithelium results in a short-term increase in proliferation of luminal cells (Wu et al., 2007; Xie et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016a), indicating a role for AR in normal prostate homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by citations.

claim: AR can act as a master regulator of prostate epithelial specification in a fibroblast reprogramming assay.
source: Importantly, AR can act as a master regulator of prostate epithelial specification in a fibroblast reprogramming assay (Talos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by a citation.

claim: Treatment failure following anti-androgen therapies is frequently associated with the appearance of AR-negative tumor cells.
source: However, treatment failure following such anti-androgen therapies is frequently associated with the appearance of AR-negative tumor cells, which are typically associated with highly aggressive lethal disease (Beltran et al., 2014; Vlachostergios et al., 2017; Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by citations.

claim: AR-negative CRPC can contain large regions displaying a neuroendocrine phenotype (CRPC-NE).
source: In some cases, this AR-negative CRPC contain large regions displaying a neuroendocrine phenotype (CRPC-NE) (Beltran et al., 2016, 2014; Ku et al., 2017; Mu et al., 2017; Zou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by citations.

claim: CARNs can generate both luminal and basal progeny in vivo following androgen administration.
source: Following androgen administration to induce prostate regeneration, CARNs can generate both luminal and basal progeny in vivo, as well as in renal grafting and organoid assays (Chua et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by citations from the authors' previous work.

claim: CARNs express AR.
source: Although CARNs express AR (Wang et al., 2009), it has been unclear whether AR is required for any or all the progenitor properties of CARNs
evidence: This is stated as background information supported by a citation from the authors' previous work.

claim: The percentage of lineage-marked YFP-positive cells (CARNs) was not significantly different between control and AR-deleted mice.
source: We found that the percentage of lineage-marked YFP-positive cells, corresponding to CARNs, was not significantly different (p=0.51) between the control (0.36 ± 0.17%, n = 5 mice) and AR-deleted mice (0.31 ± 0.06%, n = 5 mice) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on FACS analysis of mouse prostate tissue, with statistical analysis showing no significant difference.

claim: 87.1% of YFP-positive cells in AR-deleted mice were AR-negative, indicating high efficiency of AR deletion.
source: Notably, we found that 87.1% of the YFP-positive cells in Nkx3.1CreERT2/+; Arflox/Y; R26R-YFP/+ mice (n = 344/395 cells in four mice) were AR-negative, indicating that AR deletion occurred with high efficiency.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining analysis.

claim: YFP-positive cells in AR-deleted mice expressed luminal markers cytokeratins 8 and 18 (CK8 and CK18).
source: Furthermore, these YFP-positive cells expressed the luminal markers cytokeratins 8 and 18 (CK8 and CK18), but not cytokeratin 5 (CK5) and p63, indicating that AR deletion does not alter the luminal phenotype of CARNs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: YFP-positive cells in AR-deleted mice did not express basal markers cytokeratin 5 (CK5) and p63.
source: Furthermore, these YFP-positive cells expressed the luminal markers cytokeratins 8 and 18 (CK8 and CK18), but not cytokeratin 5 (CK5) and p63, indicating that AR deletion does not alter the luminal phenotype of CARNs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AR deletion does not alter the luminal phenotype of CARNs.
source: Furthermore, these YFP-positive cells expressed the luminal markers cytokeratins 8 and 18 (CK8 and CK18), but not cytokeratin 5 (CK5) and p63, indicating that AR deletion does not alter the luminal phenotype of CARNs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the marker expression data.

claim: At 14 and 28 days after testosterone administration, control prostates contained many YFP-expressing cell clusters with more than 4 cells.
source: However, at 14 and 28 days, the control prostates contained many YFP-expressing cell clusters with more than 4 cells, whereas the prostates with AR-deleted CARNs mostly contained YFP-expressing single cells or doublets (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on analysis of YFP+ cell clusters during regeneration, shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: At 14 and 28 days after testosterone administration, prostates with AR-deleted CARNs mostly contained YFP-expressing single cells or doublets.
source: However, at 14 and 28 days, the control prostates contained many YFP-expressing cell clusters with more than 4 cells, whereas the prostates with AR-deleted CARNs mostly contained YFP-expressing single cells or doublets (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on analysis of YFP+ cell clusters during regeneration, shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: When BrdU was administered from days 1 through 4 of regeneration, BrdU+YFP+ cells were detected in control prostates (50.9 ± 11.8%, n = 3 mice).
source: When BrdU was administered from days 1 through 4 of regeneration, we could readily detect BrdU+YFP+ cells in the control prostates (50.9 ± 11.8%, n = 3 mice) as well as AR-deleted prostates (62.9 ± 14.9%, n = 3 mice) (Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on BrdU incorporation experiments, shown in Figure 3C,E.

claim: When BrdU was administered from days 1 through 4 of regeneration, BrdU+YFP+ cells were detected in AR-deleted prostates (62.9 ± 14.9%, n = 3 mice).
source: When BrdU was administered from days 1 through 4 of regeneration, we could readily detect BrdU+YFP+ cells in the control prostates (50.9 ± 11.8%, n = 3 mice) as well as AR-deleted prostates (62.9 ± 14.9%, n = 3 mice) (Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on BrdU incorporation experiments, shown in Figure 3C,E.

claim: When BrdU was administered from days 11 through 14, BrdU+YFP+ cells were detected in control prostates (11.1 ± 6.2%, n = 3 mice).
source: In contrast, when BrdU was administered from days 11 through 14, we could only detect BrdU+YFP+ cells in the control prostates (11.1 ± 6.2%, n = 3 mice), but not in the AR-deleted prostates (0%, n = 3 mice) (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on BrdU incorporation experiments, shown in Figure 3D,F.

claim: When BrdU was administered from days 11 through 14, BrdU+YFP+ cells were not detected in AR-deleted prostates (0%, n = 3 mice).
source: In contrast, when BrdU was administered from days 11 through 14, we could only detect BrdU+YFP+ cells in the control prostates (11.1 ± 6.2%, n = 3 mice), but not in the AR-deleted prostates (0%, n = 3 mice) (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on BrdU incorporation experiments, shown in Figure 3D,F.

claim: AR-deleted CARNs and/or their progeny have a defect in proliferation during later stages of regeneration.
source: This difference suggests that AR-deleted CARNs and/or their progeny have a defect in proliferation during later stages of regeneration, consistent with the analysis of YFP+ cluster size (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the BrdU incorporation data.

claim: There was an increase in the percentage of basal cells within the YFP+ population in AR-deleted mice.
source: Notably, although YFP-expressing basal cells could be readily identified in both control and AR-deleted prostates, there was an increase in the percentage of basal cells within the YFP+ population in the AR-deleted mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Using the basal marker CK5, 2.1% of YFP+ cells in control mice were CK5+AR+YFP+ versus 19.2% CK5+AR–YFP+ in AR-deleted mice.
source: This difference was evident using either the basal marker CK5 (2.1% CK5+AR+YFP+ versus 19.2% CK5+AR–YFP+) or p63 (3.5% p63+AR+YFP+ versus 14.6% p63+AR–YFP+) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Using the basal marker p63, 3.5% of YFP+ cells in control mice were p63+AR+YFP+ versus 14.6% p63+AR–YFP+ in AR-deleted mice.
source: This difference was evident using either the basal marker CK5 (2.1% CK5+AR+YFP+ versus 19.2% CK5+AR–YFP+) or p63 (3.5% p63+AR+YFP+ versus 14.6% p63+AR–YFP+) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: AR-deleted CARNs favor generation of basal progeny and/or there is decreased proliferation or survival of luminal progeny during regeneration.
source: These findings indicate that AR-deleted CARNs favor generation of basal progeny and/or that there is decreased proliferation or survival of luminal progeny during regeneration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on basal cell percentages.

claim: Both control and AR-deleted CARNs could generate prostate ducts in renal grafting assays.
source: We found that both control and AR-deleted CARNs could generate prostate ducts (Figure 3H), but that the AR-deleted CARN-s were significantly less efficient (12.5% graft efficiency, n = 16) compared to the control CARNs (p=0.003; 68.8% graft efficiency, n = 16), consistent with a proliferation defect in the AR-deleted CARNs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on renal grafting experiments shown in Figure 3H.

claim: AR-deleted CARNs were significantly less efficient at generating prostate ducts (12.5% graft efficiency, n = 16) compared to control CARNs (68.8% graft efficiency, n = 16).
source: We found that both control and AR-deleted CARNs could generate prostate ducts (Figure 3H), but that the AR-deleted CARN-s were significantly less efficient (12.5% graft efficiency, n = 16) compared to the control CARNs (p=0.003; 68.8% graft efficiency, n = 16), consistent with a proliferation defect in the AR-deleted CARNs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on renal grafting experiments shown in Figure 3H, with statistical significance (p=0.003).

claim: APCA and ADCA cell lines were morphologically indistinguishable under culture conditions.
source: Under these conditions, we found that the APCA (n = 2) and ADCA (n = 2) lines were morphologically indistinguishable (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on microscopic observation of cell lines shown in Figure 4A.

claim: APCA and ADCA cell lines were comprised of a mixture of cells expressing basal (CK5) or luminal (CK8) markers or both, as well as Foxa1.
source: These cell lines were comprised of a mixture of cells expressing basal (CK5) or luminal (CK8) markers or both, as well as Foxa1, an epithelial marker that encodes a transcriptional partner of AR (Gao et al., 2003; He et al., 2010) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both APCA and ADCA lines showed robust proliferation at similar levels.
source: Furthermore, both the APCA and ADCA lines showed robust proliferation at similar levels, as demonstrated by Ki67 immunostaining, CellTiter-Glo assays, and colony formation in the presence or absence of DHT (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on multiple proliferation assays shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The relative plating efficiency for AR– CARNs compared to AR+ CARNs is 7.4%.
source: After correcting for the 87.1% efficiency of recombination of the AR-floxed allele in vivo, these data indicate that the relative plating efficiency for the AR– CARNs compared to AR+ CARNs is 7.4%, consistent with the decreased grafting efficiency of AR– CARNs.
evidence: This is a calculated result based on single-cell sorting experiments.

claim: APCA lines could generate prostate ducts in tissue recombination assays (100% efficiency, n = 10 grafts with two lines).
source: We found that the APCA lines could generate prostate ducts (n = 10 grafts with two lines; 100% efficiency), some with evidence of secretions, whereas the ADCA lines (n = 6 grafts with one line; 67% efficiency) generated ducts that lacked prostate secretions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on tissue recombination/renal grafting experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ADCA lines generated prostate ducts in tissue recombination assays (67% efficiency, n = 6 grafts with one line) that lacked prostate secretions.
source: We found that the APCA lines could generate prostate ducts (n = 10 grafts with two lines; 100% efficiency), some with evidence of secretions, whereas the ADCA lines (n = 6 grafts with one line; 67% efficiency) generated ducts that lacked prostate secretions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on tissue recombination/renal grafting experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tamoxifen treatment of APCA cell grafts resulted in decreased efficiency of graft formation (42% versus 100% efficiency).
source: We found that tamoxifen treatment resulted in grafts containing prostate ducts composed of a mixture of AR-positive and negative cells, but with a decreased efficiency of graft formation relative to the same APCA lines in the absence of tamoxifen (42% versus 100% efficiency) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on tissue recombination/renal grafting experiments with tamoxifen-induced AR deletion shown in Figure 4D.

claim: AR deletion decreases the efficiency of prostate duct formation by CARN-derived cells.
source: Together with our previous finding that CARNs display increased organoid formation efficiency relative to other luminal cells (Chua et al., 2014), these findings support the identification of CARNs as a distinct luminal population with stem/progenitor properties, and highlight the complexity of AR functions in the epithelial and stromal compartments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the grafting experiments with APCA and ADCA cells.

claim: The difference in duct formation efficiency between ADCA and APCA cells is likely due to a non-cell-autonomous effect mediated by the urogenital mesenchyme in grafts.
source: Notably, since ADCA cells do not display a growth disadvantage relative to APCA cells in culture, this difference in duct formation is likely to be due to a non-cell-autonomous effect mediated by the urogenital mesenchyme in grafts.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that ADCA cells grow normally in culture but show reduced duct formation in grafts.

claim: ADCA signature shows up-regulation of gene sets involved in DNA replication and repair pathways, as well as cell cycle and apoptosis.
source: Using the resulting ADCA signature to examine pathway enrichment by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005), we found up-regulation of gene sets involved in DNA replication and repair pathways, as well as cell cycle and apoptosis (Figure 5A), suggesting that cellular proliferation and survival are affected by AR deletion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on RNA-seq and GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The ADCA signature shows enrichment for up-regulated genes when compared with a signature of AR-null mouse prostate luminal cells.
source: We also compared the ADCA signature with a signature defined between expression profiles of AR-null and AR-positive mouse prostate luminal cells (Xie et al., 2017) and found enrichment for up-regulated genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on cross-species GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ADCA signature shows no significant enrichment when compared with a signature of human prostate luminal versus basal epithelial cells.
source: Next, we performed a cross-species comparison of the ADCA signature with a signature defined between profiles of human prostate luminal and basal epithelial cells (Zhang et al., 2016b) and found that there was no significant enrichment in either tail (Figure 5C), indicating that AR deletion does not drive APCA cells towards a specific lineage.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on cross-species GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: AR deletion does not drive APCA cells towards a specific lineage.
source: Next, we performed a cross-species comparison of the ADCA signature with a signature defined between profiles of human prostate luminal and basal epithelial cells (Zhang et al., 2016b) and found that there was no significant enrichment in either tail (Figure 5C), indicating that AR deletion does not drive APCA cells towards a specific lineage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ADCA signature shows enrichment for up-regulated genes when compared to a signature of CRPC from Best and colleagues.
source: In particular, we observed enrichment for up-regulated genes when compared to a signature of CRPC from Best and colleagues (Best et al., 2005), as well as to a signature of metastatic CRPC from Stanbrough and colleagues (Stanbrough et al., 2006) (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on cross-species GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The ADCA signature shows enrichment for up-regulated genes when compared to a signature of metastatic CRPC from Stanbrough and colleagues.
source: In particular, we observed enrichment for up-regulated genes when compared to a signature of CRPC from Best and colleagues (Best et al., 2005), as well as to a signature of metastatic CRPC from Stanbrough and colleagues (Stanbrough et al., 2006) (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on cross-species GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The ADCA signature shows strong enrichment when compared to a signature of CRPC-NE versus non-neuroendocrine CRPC from Beltran and colleagues.
source: Moreover, we observed a strong enrichment when compared to a signature from Beltran and colleagues (Beltran et al., 2016) defined between CRPC with neuroendocrine differentiation (CRPC-NE) and non-neuroendocrine CRPC (Figure 5F), consistent with our observation of pathway enrichment for gene sets corresponding to axon guidance and small-cell lung cancer (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on cross-species GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: NP-CARN controls displayed high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN).
source: We found that AR deletion resulted in a significant difference between the NP-CARN and NPA-CARN phenotypes, as the NP-CARN controls displayed high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN), whereas the NPA-CARN prostates showed a weak phenotype corresponding to diffuse hyperplasia with mild inflammation and increased apoptosis, (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on histological analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: NPA-CARN prostates showed a weak phenotype corresponding to diffuse hyperplasia with mild inflammation and increased apoptosis.
source: We found that AR deletion resulted in a significant difference between the NP-CARN and NPA-CARN phenotypes, as the NP-CARN controls displayed high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN), whereas the NPA-CARN prostates showed a weak phenotype corresponding to diffuse hyperplasia with mild inflammation and increased apoptosis, (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on histological analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: NPA-CARN prostates displayed a decreased proliferative index (2.7%, n = 3) relative to NP-CARN (9.2%, n = 3).
source: Furthermore, the NPA-CARN prostates displayed a decreased proliferative index relative to NP-CARN (2.7%, n = 3 vs. 9.2%, n = 3), as well as increased apoptosis (2.6%, n = 3 vs. 0.7%, n = 3) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on Ki67 staining analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NPA-CARN prostates displayed increased apoptosis (2.6%, n = 3) relative to NP-CARN (0.7%, n = 3).
source: Furthermore, the NPA-CARN prostates displayed a decreased proliferative index relative to NP-CARN (2.7%, n = 3 vs. 9.2%, n = 3), as well as increased apoptosis (2.6%, n = 3 vs. 0.7%, n = 3) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on cleaved caspase-3 staining analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: AR is required for tumor initiation following Pten deletion in CARNs.
source: Taken together, findings indicate that AR is required for tumor initiation following Pten deletion in CARNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NP-CARN and NPA-CARN experiments.

claim: AR deletion did not affect tumor initiation following combined deletion of Pten and activation of oncogenic KrasG12D.
source: In contrast, AR deletion did not affect tumor initiation following combined deletion of Pten and activation of the oncogenic KrasG12D allele.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on comparison of NPK-CARN and NPKA-CARN mice.

claim: Both NPK-CARN and NPKA-CARN tumors displayed high proliferative indices (20%, n = 3 vs. 19%, n = 3).
source: Furthermore, both NPK-CARN and NPKA-CARN tumors displayed high proliferative indices (20%, n = 3 vs. 19%, n = 3) and low frequencies of apoptosis (0.9%, n = 3 vs. 0.8%, n = 3) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on Ki67 staining analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both NPK-CARN and NPKA-CARN tumors displayed low frequencies of apoptosis (0.9%, n = 3 vs. 0.8%, n = 3).
source: Furthermore, both NPK-CARN and NPKA-CARN tumors displayed high proliferative indices (20%, n = 3 vs. 19%, n = 3) and low frequencies of apoptosis (0.9%, n = 3 vs. 0.8%, n = 3) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on cleaved caspase-3 staining analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All NPKA-CARN tumors contained a low but variable percentage of synaptophysin-positive neuroendocrine cells among total epithelial cells (0.7%, n = 3).
source: Notably, we observed an important difference between the NPK-CARN and NPKA-CARN tumors, as all the NPKA-CARN tumors contained a low but variable percentage of synaptophysin-positive neuroendocrine cells among total epithelial cells (0.7%, n = 3), which were never observed in the NPK-CARN controls (0%, n = 3) (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on synaptophysin staining analysis shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Synaptophysin-positive neuroendocrine cells were never observed in NPK-CARN controls (0%, n = 3).
source: Notably, we observed an important difference between the NPK-CARN and NPKA-CARN tumors, as all the NPKA-CARN tumors contained a low but variable percentage of synaptophysin-positive neuroendocrine cells among total epithelial cells (0.7%, n = 3), which were never observed in the NPK-CARN controls (0%, n = 3) (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on synaptophysin staining analysis shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Synaptophysin-positive cells in NPKA-CARN tumors co-expressed YFP.
source: Since the synaptophysin-postive cells co-expressed YFP (Figure 6E), we conclude that transformed AR-negative CARNs can give rise to neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Transformed AR-negative CARNs can give rise to neuroendocrine cells.
source: Since the synaptophysin-postive cells co-expressed YFP (Figure 6E), we conclude that transformed AR-negative CARNs can give rise to neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that synaptophysin-positive cells co-express YFP in NPKA-CARN tumors.

claim: The intrinsic castration-resistance of CARNs is independent of AR function.
source: Taken together, our analyses have defined specific roles for AR in regulating the progenitor properties of CARNs, and indicate that the intrinsic castration-resistance of CARNs is independent of AR function.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the overall findings.

claim: Targeted deletion of AR does not affect the percentage of CARNs.
source: We find that targeted deletion of AR does not affect the percentage of CARNs, their luminal marker expression, or their ability to generate basal cells during androgen-mediated regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Targeted deletion of AR does not affect luminal marker expression of CARNs.
source: We find that targeted deletion of AR does not affect the percentage of CARNs, their luminal marker expression, or their ability to generate basal cells during androgen-mediated regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Targeted deletion of AR does not affect the ability of CARNs to generate basal cells during androgen-mediated regeneration.
source: We find that targeted deletion of AR does not affect the percentage of CARNs, their luminal marker expression, or their ability to generate basal cells during androgen-mediated regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: There are fewer luminal progeny from AR-deleted CARNs during regeneration in vivo.
source: However, there are fewer luminal progeny from AR-deleted CARNs during regeneration in vivo, and there is a decreased efficiency of prostate duct formation by both AR-deleted CARNs and ADCA cells in renal grafts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: There is a decreased efficiency of prostate duct formation by AR-deleted CARNs in renal grafts.
source: However, there are fewer luminal progeny from AR-deleted CARNs during regeneration in vivo, and there is a decreased efficiency of prostate duct formation by both AR-deleted CARNs and ADCA cells in renal grafts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: There is a decreased efficiency of prostate duct formation by ADCA cells in renal grafts.
source: However, there are fewer luminal progeny from AR-deleted CARNs during regeneration in vivo, and there is a decreased efficiency of prostate duct formation by both AR-deleted CARNs and ADCA cells in renal grafts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: AR deletion in CARNs may primarily affect the proliferation and/or survival of their luminal progeny in vivo.
source: Thus, AR deletion in CARNs may primarily affect the proliferation and/or survival of their luminal progeny in vivo, although an effect on CARNs themselves cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: AR activity may cell-autonomously regulate the proliferation of luminal progeny of CARNs.
source: One possible explanation is that AR activity may cell-autonomously regulate the proliferation of luminal progeny of CARNs; alternatively, however, stromal remodeling during later stages of regeneration may alter non-cell autonomous signals that regulate luminal proliferation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed proliferation defect.

claim: Stromal remodeling during later stages of regeneration may alter non-cell autonomous signals that regulate luminal proliferation.
